items.question: If Palantir didn't exist, what kind of company or work would you be most excited and interested in working at/on? (Approx. 200 words)
items.problem: Expected "I would want to work on infrastructure for scientific research and evaluation. Over the past year I've independently studied how research gets funded and selected, reading the history from patronage through the German research university, Bell Labs, the postwar NIH/NSF project-grant model, and newer structures like DARPA, ARPA-H, and Focused Research Organizations, and interviewing researchers, research administrators, economists, and science-policy people. I started out thinking grant-writing time was the main constraint on science. I now think the bigger effect is selection: researchers learn which ideas are legible enough to survive review, and difficult-to-justify ideas may never get attempted. The part that interests me most now is that AI is making generation cheap while judgment stays scarce. Reviewers have limited time and domain expertise is expensive, so output can grow much faster than the capacity to evaluate it. I got interested in this concretely at Intelehealth, where I designed an evaluation framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard using stratified sampling to surface systematic failure modes. Generating an answer was easy; deciding whether to trust it was the hard part. I'd be excited to build systems for methodological validation, provenance, uncertainty, evidence tracing, and escalation to human experts."; page shows "(empty)"

items.question: What is the hardest technical challenge you've faced as part of work experience or a personal project? (Approx. 200 words)
items.problem: Expected "The hardest one was estimating sleep without a wearable for ClarityAtlas, the iOS health product I built as technical lead at Open Health Intelligence. Most sleep features assume a device on the user's wrist. Our pilot users at Hopkins were students with phones and nothing else, so I had to infer sleep passively from phone-interaction patterns plus HealthKit and Core Motion signals like step count, gait speed, and movement patterns. The difficulty was that none of those signals directly observe sleep. Absence of interaction can mean sleeping, or a dead battery, or a phone left on a desk while someone studies in the library. I had to decide what the system should do when the evidence genuinely did not support a conclusion, rather than emitting a confident number that would quietly teach users to distrust the whole product. I built the estimation pipeline in Swift with Supabase on the backend, and separately built a "Sleep Twins" matching service over standardized behavioral features with weighted distance so users could compare against similar people rather than population averages. We shipped it into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users, and their feedback is what forced me to tighten the failure cases."; page shows "(empty)"

items.question: Tell us one thing that’s not on your resume that you’re proud of.
items.problem: Expected "During Hopkins' Lighting of the Quads, my cofounders and I realized President Ron Daniels was nearby. We followed him to Garland Hall, saw him through the locked doors, and knocked until someone let us get a few minutes to pitch ClarityAtlas. It was mildly ridiculous, and it worked. That conversation eventually turned into a formal meeting months later where we presented to him and to leadership from the Johns Hopkins Data Science and AI Institute. I'm proud of it because I spent a long time believing the technical work was the hard part. Building the iOS app, the sleep-estimation pipeline, and the matching backend was work I already knew how to do. Getting the product in front of the people who could actually make it real at an institution was the part I had no template for, and it mostly came down to being willing to look foolish on a cold night. Recruiting pilot users, explaining repeatedly why the thing should exist, and knocking on a locked door all turned out to matter as much as the code."; page shows "(empty)"

items.question: At Palantir we have two main Software Engineering roles: Forward Deployed Software Engineer and Software Engineer. Which of these roles resonates the most with your job search and why? More details found here: https://blog.palantir.com/dev-versus-delta-demystifying-engineering-roles-at-palantir-ad44c2a6e87
items.problem: Expected "Software Engineer resonates more with what I'm looking for, which is why I'm applying to Infrastructure. The work I've found most satisfying is owning the core system rather than adapting an existing one per deployment. At Summer Atlantic Capital I built and own major parts of the data and ML infrastructure for an anomaly-detection system: the repository and CI scaffold, the event-ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI microservice, and the public detection API, alongside the temporal sequence modeling and a learning-to-rank layer for alert prioritization. Similarly, in my job-application agent I cared most about the architecture: SQLite as the single source of truth because browser automation gets dangerous when state diverges across processes, an explicit state machine per application, and fail-closed environment flags for every mutating capability. That said, I don't want to build infrastructure with no view of the user. What pushed me toward prioritization and an RAG explanation layer on the anomaly system was that an alert system producing too many alerts creates a second problem instead of solving the first. I want to be on the core engineering side while staying close to how the thing actually fails in production."; page shows "(empty)"
